title: Thinking About Perpendicular Bisectors
author: Paul Rowlandson
summary: Paul Rowlandson traces how his teaching of compass-and-ruler perpendicular bisector constructions evolved from a pure step-by-step memorised procedure toward a reasoning-based approach built on the properties of circles, kites, and isosceles triangles. He found the original step-by-step method left students unable to adapt to unfamiliar constructions, and an early attempt to add conceptual discussion overloaded students who were simultaneously wrestling with compass dexterity. His solution was to move teacher-led exploration onto GeoGebra, letting students first reason about what happens when two circles intersect -- forming a kite whose diagonals are perpendicular -- before touching a compass at all, so the concept and the motor skill are no longer competing for the same attention. Students then deduce, through guided variation and questioning, first how to construct a perpendicular line and then a perpendicular bisector, arriving at the standard procedure themselves rather than being handed it up front.
points: Rowlandson's diagnosis of his own early teaching is precise: teaching constructions as memorised step-by-step procedures worked for the exact taught construction but left students unable to adapt to the many other constructions GCSE exams actually demand.

His key structural insight is separating the conceptual load from the motor-skill load: doing the reasoning first in GeoGebra (kites, circle properties, perpendicular diagonals) before introducing a physical pair of compasses, so students aren't fighting both problems at once.

The deduction sequence he builds -- circles intersecting, forming a kite, kite diagonals being perpendicular, therefore how to construct a perpendicular line, therefore a perpendicular bisector -- lets students derive the standard procedure themselves rather than receiving it as a rule to memorise.

He reports a durable payoff: even though he still summarised a step-by-step method at the end of lessons, most students didn't need it, and they transferred the underlying reasoning to later, related constructions like angle bisectors.
quotes: I was never satisfied with simply teaching constructions as step-by-step processes for pupils to follow, reproduce, and memorise.
Even when pupils successfully reproduced and memorised my step-by-step process, I found they often struggled to adapt it when they faced with other, less familiar constructions.
It felt like the compasses were a distraction from learning how to construct perpendicular bisectors.

Rather than the sole objective of the lesson being to 'learn how to construct a perpendicular bisector using a pair of compasses and a ruler', the primary objective would be to 'explore what happens when circles intersect'.

One of these is that kites have a line of symmetry which (in the case of these constructions) passes through the centre of each circle. Additionally, the two diagonals of a kite are always perpendicular.
While I did usually summarise by outlining a step-by-step method towards the end of the lesson, most pupils didn’t seem to need it.
